summary: This experimental document specifies the Dynamic Source Routing protocol for multi-hop wireless ad hoc networks, for routing unicast IPv4 packets. Nodes self-organize without infrastructure, using on-demand Route Discovery and Route Maintenance. It is designed for networks of up to about two hundred nodes.

plainLanguage.summary: A bunch of phones with no tower pass notes hand to hand. The sender writes the whole route on the note, and they ask around for a route only when they need one.

subtitle: Source routing for wireless mobile networks without infrastructure.

tldr.problem: Mobile devices in wireless networks need to route packets to each other without central infrastructure, and network topology changes rapidly as devices move.
tldr.mechanism: DSR uses source routing where the sender includes the complete path in each packet header, and discovers new routes on demand using broadcast requests when needed.
tldr.outcome: Overhead scales to zero when the network is stable, routes adapt quickly to mobility, and nodes can learn routes by overhearing other packets.

facts.label: Route discovery scope
facts.value: Controlled by hop limit in IP header

facts.label: State type
facts.value: Soft state; easily recoverable if lost

today: RFC 4728 is Experimental and has not been obsoleted. DSR was designed for small mobile ad hoc networks and has been studied extensively through simulation and testbed deployment. The protocol remains a reference design for on-demand routing in wireless networks, though deployment is limited and other MANET protocols have been standardized.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
Dynamic Source Routing (DSR) is a routing protocol for wireless networks where computers move around and have no central infrastructure like a WiFi tower. Unlike traditional routing, DSR lets each sender decide the exact path its packets take by listing the hops in the packet header itself.

The protocol has two main mechanisms: Route Discovery finds a path to a destination when needed (not periodically), and Route Maintenance detects and handles broken links. Because DSR operates entirely on demand and uses soft state (state that is easily recoverable), overhead shrinks to nearly zero when the network stabilizes. The sender controls routes, enabling load balancing and quick adaptation to network changes.
sections.plainLanguage: When you want to send a note to someone, you write the list of people who should pass it along. You only ask others for routes when you need one, and you can quickly learn shortcuts by watching how others send their notes.

sections.title: Route Discovery and Maintenance
sections.content:
Route Discovery happens when a node wants to send to a destination it does not know a route to. The sender broadcasts a Route Request locally. Each intermediate node that receives it appends its address to a route record and rebroadcasts, unless it is the target or has already seen this request. When the target receives the request, it sends back a Route Reply containing the accumulated path. The sender may then cache multiple routes and use them for subsequent packets.

Once a source route is in use, Route Maintenance detects link failures through acknowledgements (from the link layer, passive overhearing, or explicit requests). When a link breaks, the node at that hop sends a Route Error back to the sender, which removes that link from its cache and either tries another route or initiates a new discovery. This rapid reaction avoids long timeouts when topology changes.

DSR caches routes learned not only from discovery but from overheard packet headers, reducing discovery overhead. If nodes can hear packets they are not the target of (promiscuous mode), they learn forward-direction links and can cache shortcuts. Route caching trades memory for quick adaptation to mobility.
sections.plainLanguage: To find someone, you broadcast a message asking for a route. Each person who hears it adds their name and passes it on. When it reaches the target, they send back the path they saw. When a link breaks, you learn about it and try a different route or ask again.

sections.title: Data Structures and Packet Format
sections.content:
Each node maintains several data structures. The Route Cache stores known paths to destinations, either as complete paths (path cache) or as a graph of individual links (link cache). Both designs can work; link caches are more powerful but require graph search algorithms like Dijkstra's. The cache has a timeout so old routes expire, and a Send Buffer holds packets awaiting routes. A Route Request Table tracks ongoing discoveries by target address, recording the last request time and implementing exponential backoff so nodes do not flood the network with requests to unreachable destinations.

Packets carry a DSR Options Header with several option types: Route Request (for discovery broadcasts), Route Reply (returning the path), Route Error (reporting broken links), Acknowledgement Request and Acknowledgement (for link-layer confirmation), and DSR Source Route (the actual path being used). Each option has a fixed header and variable-length fields.

DSR supports an optional Flow State Extension that establishes flows with fixed IDs, allowing most packets to omit the full source route header. This trades more state for fewer bytes on the wire when a flow is stable. Nodes detect loops in flow-state mode by tracking sequence numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: Each phone remembers the routes it has found and the people it has asked. When it wants to send, it puts the path right in the message header. If a link breaks, the message bounces back with an error.

sections.title: Protocol Operation and Optimizations
sections.content:
When originating a packet, a node searches its Route Cache for a suitable route. If found, it adds the source route option to the packet and sends it. Intermediate nodes simply follow the route in the header without routing lookups. When receiving a packet with a DSR Options Header, each node processes its route record and may cache the information for future use.

DSR includes several optimizations to reduce overhead. Packet Salvaging allows an intermediate node that detects a broken link to salvage the packet by removing the failed hop from the route and forwarding it along the shortened path, avoiding the cost of a retransmission. Automatic Route Shortening lets a node overhearing a packet sent by another node, when that node is not the immediate next hop but is named later in the route, send a gratuitous Route Reply offering the shorter path. The Route Request Hop Limit mechanism controls how far a discovery request spreads, using the IP TTL field; a node can expand the limit on retry if the initial search fails.

All routing state is soft state: nodes discover routes as needed, and losing cached information does not break the protocol. Nodes can use link-layer checksums to detect and discard corrupted packets, and DSR works with both bidirectional and unidirectional links (though some MAC protocols like IEEE 802.11 restrict unicast to bidirectional links due to their own requirements).
sections.plainLanguage: The packet header tells each hop exactly where to send it next. If a link breaks mid-route, the node can try a shortcut it knows about, saving time. Overhearing other routes lets you learn the network faster, and you only ask for directions when you really need them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DSR assumes all nodes in the ad hoc network cooperate fully; each node must be willing to forward packets for others. The protocol does not include authentication of routing information. A malicious or compromised node can forge routes, redirect packets, drop packets, replay old routing messages, or inject false route errors to disrupt communication. These attacks are not addressed in DSR itself but would need to be handled by upper-layer security protocols or a trusted routing layer.

The soft-state design makes DSR robust to transient faults: a node that crashes and reboots can rejoin quickly. However, it also means the protocol trusts that nodes implementing it correctly maintain sequence numbers in their Route Request IDs to avoid infinite loops after reboots. The optional Flow State Extension adds sequence numbers to detect loop attacks within a single flow.
sections.plainLanguage: DSR trusts that everyone playing the game follows the rules. A bad actor could tell lies about routes or drop your messages, but DSR itself does not have locks and guards to stop that.
